sengoku_daimyo: Ashikaga shoguns of the Muromachi shogunate

meiji_transition.summary: Kyoto-fu was established in 1868 and absorbed neighboring prefectures in 1871; in 1876 the five Tango districts and Tanba's Amata District came over from Toyooka Prefecture, giving today's long north–south shape.
meiji_transition.boundary_note: Kyoto Prefecture combines Yamashiro (the basin), eastern Tanba and Tango (the Sea of Japan coast) — which is why it stretches from Kyoto city all the way to Amanohashidate.

history_timeline.title: Heian-kyō
history_timeline.summary: In 794 Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō, the imperial seat for the next thousand years; The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book were born here.

history_timeline.title: The Rokuhara Tandai
history_timeline.summary: Power moved east to Kamakura, but Kyoto remained the seat of the court; after the 1221 Jōkyū War the shogunate set up the Rokuhara Tandai to watch over it.

history_timeline.title: Kitayama and Higashiyama cultures
history_timeline.summary: Ashikaga Takauji opened his shogunate in Kyoto; Yoshimitsu built the Golden Pavilion (1397) and Yoshimasa, in his later years, the Silver Pavilion — the Kitayama and Higashiyama cultures in turn.

history_timeline.title: The Ōnin War
history_timeline.summary: The Ōnin War of 1467 reduced Kyoto to ashes and began the Sengoku era; Nobunaga's march on the capital, the Honnō-ji Incident and Hideyoshi's Jurakudai all played out here.

history_timeline.title: City of the emperor
history_timeline.summary: With politics gone east, Kyoto became the city of the emperor, nobles, temples and crafts, where Nishijin weaving and Kyō-yūzen flourished; in the late Edo period loyalists and the Shinsengumi clashed here.

history_timeline.title: The old capital reborn
history_timeline.summary: After the emperor moved east in 1869, Kyoto revived with the Lake Biwa Canal and Japan's first streetcar; its historic monuments became World Heritage in 1994.

landmarks.name: Amanohashidate
landmarks.note: One of the Three Views of Japan

dialect.name: Kyō-kotoba (Kyoto speech)
dialect.features: Soft and indirect, with '-dosu' and '-haru' endings; people speak obliquely — 'Would you like some bubuzuke?' may actually mean 'time to go home'.

phrases.meaning: Would you like some tea over rice?
phrases.note: a polite hint that it's time to leave

guide.opening: I witnessed the great fires of Heian-kyō. Which tale of the past would you like to hear?

regional_meme.title: Kyoto's 'last war'
regional_meme.text: Old Kyotoites are said to mean the Ōnin War (1467) by 'the last war'; the 'bubuzuke' hint to leave is another classic.

regional_meme.title: 'That's not Kyoto'
regional_meme.text: To people in central Kyoto, the north of the prefecture (Tango, Tanba) — and even the city's outskirts — 'aren't really Kyoto'.

hero_persona.name: Akechi Mitsuhide
hero_persona.title: Rebel of the Honnō-ji Incident
hero_persona.opening_line: I am Akechi Hyūga-no-kami Mitsuhide. 'The enemy is at Honnō-ji'… why did I raise my army? Everyone has a theory — would you hear mine?
hero_persona.tone_prompt: refined and somber, cultured; speaks obliquely of the Honnō-ji Incident; note that there is no settled view of his motives

ramen.broth: Shōyu (chicken and pork bone with back fat)
ramen.toppings: Kujō green onion, chashu, back fat
ramen.highlight: Kyotoites actually love rich flavors — both back-fat shōyu and thick chicken paitan were born here

sake.taste_profile: Light & sweet: the soft 'feminine sake' of Fushimi's soft water
